title: Hall, Yard and Docks
text:
1. Harborwick 3PL Ltd. operates from a single site in Port Sellow, Alveria, comprising one single-storey warehouse hall with an attached office annex and an enclosed yard. The site is fenced on all sides and access is controlled during operating hours.

2. The warehouse hall provides 6,000 m2 of enclosed operating floor with 10 m clear height under the roof structure. All storage, handling, picking, packing and dispatch activities take place inside the hall, except for vehicle parking, manoeuvring and dock approach, which take place in the yard.

3. A small office annex adjoining the hall houses warehouse management, shift supervision, dispatch, stock control and driver reception. Drivers and visitors report to the office annex on arrival and do not enter the operational floor unless authorised and escorted.

4. The fenced yard outside the hall covers approximately 3,500 m2. It provides circulation space for goods vehicles, marked manoeuvring lanes for dock approach, staff and visitor parking, and a marked driver waiting area. Drivers wait in the designated waiting area until called to their door and never wait inside the hall.

5. The building has 8 dock doors on one elevation, all built at 1.2 m dock height to match standard trailers and curtain-side vehicles. Each dock door is equipped with its own dock leveller for safe bridging between the building floor and the vehicle bed. Doors and levellers are maintained as part of the site equipment and any defect is reported immediately to maintenance.

6. Dock doors are strictly segregated by flow direction. Doors 1-4 are inbound only and serve receiving in Zone A. Doors 5-8 are outbound only and serve dispatch staging in Zone D. No inbound unloading takes place at an outbound door and no outbound loading takes place at an inbound door.

7. Every arriving and departing vehicle is assigned a specific door and a time slot by the dispatcher. Carriers may approach a dock only after confirmation of door number and slot. Unscheduled vehicles hold in the yard or waiting area until instructed. The dispatcher owns dock scheduling and resolves any conflict over door use.

8. Pedestrian and vehicle areas in the yard and at the docks are marked and separated. Pedestrians use only marked walkways, crossings and the waiting area, and do not cross dock manoeuvring lanes except at marked points. Internal traffic rules, aisle widths, speed limits and personal protective equipment requirements apply in full in the hall, yard and dock areas and are detailed in the relevant safety sections of this Manual.

9. The hall floor is divided into six defined operating zones, A to F, which are described in the next section. Zone boundaries, dock approaches and pedestrian routes are permanently marked on the floor and on signage. Nothing is stored, staged or parked outside its assigned zone or in a way that blocks a dock door, leveller, emergency exit or transport aisle.

title: Zones A to F
text:
1. The 6,000 m2 operating floor is divided into six fixed zones, A to F. Every activity has an assigned zone, and all staff learn the zones on day one. No goods, pallets or equipment are stored or staged outside their assigned zone, and zone boundaries, aisles and pedestrian routes are permanently marked.

2. Zone A — receiving (800 m2) serves inbound Doors 1-4. All unloading, document checking, counting and goods inspection take place here. Nothing moves past Zone A into storage until the paperwork has been checked and the goods have been inspected and booked into the system.

3. Zone B — bulk storage (2,200 m2) is the main warehouse store. It contains high-bay pallet racking providing 2,400 pallet positions. Each rack bay carries at most 2,700 kg. Where goods are block-stacked outside the racking, stacks are limited to 3 pallets high and 4.0 m in height. General ambient packed consumer goods are held here.

4. Zone C — picking (1,200 m2) holds the ground-level pick faces and flow racks from which customer orders are picked. It carries only working stock for current order picking. Before each picking shift, the pick faces in Zone C are replenished from bulk storage in Zone B, so pickers work only from replenished, system-directed faces.

5. Zone D — dispatch (900 m2) is the outbound staging area in front of outbound Doors 5-8. Only wrapped, labelled pallets that have been packed, verified and released for a specific outbound load are staged here. Pallets are staged by door and load, kept clear of levellers, aisles and emergency exits, and are loaded and sealed on instruction from the dispatcher.

6. Zone E — cold zone (300 m2) is the enclosed chilled store for temperature-sensitive goods. It is held continuously between +2 °C and +8 °C, fitted with temperature alarms, and subject to a manual temperature verification each shift. Only inspected and booked chilled goods are put away to Zone E, and cold-chain rules apply to every movement in and out.

7. Zone F — services and control (600 m2) houses value-added packing, quarantine, returns inspection and stock control functions. All returns are received and inspected here, and all damaged goods are held in quarantine here from the day they are found until a disposition decision is made.

8. Inside Zone F sits a separate ventilated hazmat cage of 60 m2. All hazardous goods are stored only in this cage and never anywhere else on site. The total quantity in the cage never exceeds 4,000 kg at any one time. Access, handling and spill response for the cage follow the dedicated hazmat procedure.

9. Material flow follows the zone sequence. Inbound goods move from Zone A to Zone B, E or F after inspection and booking; Zone B feeds Zone C; picked and packed goods move from Zone C to Zone D; returns and damaged goods move to Zone F. Staff do not bypass a zone, move unbooked goods to storage, or stage unwrapped or unlabelled pallets in Zone D.

title: Shifts and Procedures
text:
1. Harborwick 3PL Ltd. operates two fixed shifts, Monday to Friday. The morning shift runs 06:00-14:00 and the afternoon shift runs 14:00-22:00. All routine receiving, storage, picking, packing and dispatch work is planned within these windows, and the site is not routinely operated outside them.

2. There is always one shift supervisor in charge of the floor during operating hours. The shift supervisor runs the shift, directs floor staff, manages priorities across Zones A to F, and leads the initial response to any incident until management takes over.

3. The company employs around forty people in total, rostered across the two shifts to cover inbound, bulk storage, picking, dispatch, stock control, returns and packing, maintenance and dispatch planning. A small pool of floaters covers absence so that each shift remains capable of its planned workload.

4. In peak season the company adds Saturday morning overtime to clear backlog and meet client commitments. Saturday working is overtime only, is planned in advance, and is limited to the morning period required to restore flow. No regular Sunday or night working is operated.

5. Only the warehouse manager approves overtime. Shift supervisors, dispatchers and other staff do not authorise additional hours, additional shifts or extended opening on their own authority.

6. Every activity on site runs off fifteen written procedures, numbered PR-01 to PR-15. The procedures are binding on all staff, including supervisors and management. Training, daily checks, handovers and incident reviews all refer back to the applicable procedure.

7. The flow procedures cover the movement of goods in order. PR-01 Inbound receiving governs dock arrival, document checks, unloading and inspection. PR-02 Put-away to storage governs movement of booked goods to Zones B, E and F. PR-03 Replenishment of pick faces governs feeding Zone C from bulk. PR-04 Order picking governs scanner-directed picking in Zone C.

8. PR-05 Packing and labelling, PR-06 Outbound dispatch and PR-07 Returns handling complete the goods flow. PR-05 covers verification, packing and labelling after picking. PR-06 covers staging in Zone D, release, loading and sealing. PR-07 covers acceptance of returns within 14 days of delivery, inspection in Zone F and the restock, rework or scrap proposal.

9. The control and safety procedures support the flow at all times. PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts governs daily cycle counts and the annual wall-to-wall stocktake. PR-09 Damaged-goods handling governs same-day quarantine and write-off control. PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation and PR-11 Pedestrian safety in the warehouse govern trucks, aisles, walkways and protective equipment.

10. PR-12 Cold-chain handling governs the +2 °C to +8 °C regime and shift verification in Zone E. PR-13 Hazmat handling and spill response governs storage in the ventilated cage in Zone F and the 4,000 kg limit. PR-14 Emergency evacuation governs alarms, evacuation and quarterly drills with roll call. PR-15 End-of-shift handover governs transfer of status, stock issues and open incidents between shifts.

11. Where this Manual summarises a rule, the written procedure remains the working instruction. If any summary in this Manual differs from how the site is actually run as described by the owner, the owner's description prevails and the Manual is corrected.

title: Management and Supervision
text:
1. The warehouse manager is accountable for the whole site — its operations, its safety and its final sign-offs. Nothing on site operates outside the manager's accountability, whether it concerns stock accuracy, floor discipline, equipment, or compliance with procedures PR-01 to PR-15.

2. The warehouse manager sets operating priorities, rosters the two shifts, plans peak-season Saturday overtime needs, and ensures that each shift is staffed to cover inbound, storage, picking, dispatch, stock control, returns and packing, maintenance and dispatch planning.

3. The warehouse manager owns the fifteen written procedures and ensures that training, daily work, checks, handovers and incident reviews refer back to the applicable procedure. Where working practice and a written summary differ, the way the site is actually run as described by the owner prevails.

4. Final sign-offs are reserved to the warehouse manager. The manager personally signs off the annual wall-to-wall stocktake results and any damaged-goods write-off above 500 EUR. No stocktake is closed and no write-off above 500 EUR is posted without that signature.

5. Two authorisations belong only to the warehouse manager. Only the manager approves overtime, including peak-season Saturday morning working, and only the manager authorises new forklift operators. No supervisor, dispatcher or other staff member grants these approvals.

6. Each shift — mornings 06:00-14:00 and afternoons 14:00-22:00, Monday to Friday — is run by a shift supervisor. There are two shift supervisors in total, one in charge of the floor on each shift. There is always one shift supervisor in charge of the floor during operating hours.

7. The shift supervisor on duty directs all floor staff on that shift across Zones A to F. The supervisor sets the order of work between receiving, put-away, replenishment, picking, packing, dispatch, returns and stock counts, redeploys staff and floaters to cover absence or backlog, and ensures zone discipline and handover to the next shift.

8. The shift supervisor leads the initial response to any incident on the shift, including injury, damage, spill, cold-chain alarm, fire alarm or security issue. The supervisor secures people and goods, calls the required support, preserves the scene for review, and escalates to the warehouse manager without delay.

9. Within the shift, the shift supervisor approves damaged-goods write-offs up to and including 500 EUR, approves the final disposition of inspected returns — restock, rework or scrap — following the proposal from returns staff, and reviews every incident report arising on the shift before it is closed or escalated.

10. The reporting line is fixed. Floor staff report to the shift supervisor on duty for tasking, safety and incident reporting. The shift supervisor reports to the warehouse manager for performance of the shift, open stock issues, incidents, overtime need and any matter requiring a manager-only sign-off or authorisation.

title: Operational Roles
text:
1. The operational workforce totals around forty people rostered across the two shifts: 8 forklift operators, 6 inbound operators, 10 pickers, 2 stock controllers, 4 returns and packing staff, 1 maintenance technician, 2 dispatchers and 2 floaters, in addition to the warehouse manager and 2 shift supervisors. Every person works under the shift supervisor on duty and to procedures PR-01 to PR-15.

2. Forklift operators drive the company's materials-handling equipment. They operate the 6 counterbalance forklifts rated at 2.5 t for general work, the 4 reach trucks rated at 1.6 t for the high bays in Zone B, and the 8 electric and 12 hand pallet jacks for small moves. No other staff drive forklifts or reach trucks.

3. Only authorised forklift operators drive trucks. Authorisation is granted only by the warehouse manager, and no licence means no truck. Every operator completes a documented check of the truck before its first use each day, wears a seat belt whenever the truck is moving, and observes all driving, speed and pedestrian rules.

4. Inbound operators work in Zone A at inbound Doors 1-4. They receive carriers at the assigned door and slot, check delivery documents before anything is unloaded, then unload, count and inspect the goods. Only inspected goods are presented for booking into the system, and nothing moves past Zone A until paperwork and inspection are complete.

5. Pickers work in Zone C against scanner tasks issued through the 20 shared handheld WMS scanners. They pick only from replenished pick faces and flow racks fed from bulk storage, follow the scanner sequence for each customer order, and scan-verify every picked item before it is packed. Pickers do not pick from bulk racking or from unbooked stock.

6. After picking, pickers pack, label and move goods toward Zone D in line with PR-04 and PR-05. They ensure picked pallets and cartons are correctly identified, kept in their assigned zone flow, and handed over for wrapping and staging. Only wrapped, labelled pallets move to Zone D.

7. Stock controllers own inventory accuracy day to day. They run the daily cycle counts on the rotating zone schedule, perform recounts, investigate discrepancies between system and rack, and prepare adjustments for approval. No adjustment is ever posted without a second count, and the annual wall-to-wall stocktake is worked under their control for final sign-off by the manager.

8. Returns and packing staff work in Zone F. They receive returns, accept them only within 14 days of delivery, and inspect every unit. Following inspection they propose restock, rework or scrap for each return, and they carry out value-added packing work to instruction. They do not decide final disposition, which belongs to the shift supervisor.

9. Dispatchers book transport, assign every carrier a door and a time slot, and release outbound loads. They assign Doors 1-4 for inbound and Doors 5-8 for outbound, direct drivers to the marked waiting area, call vehicles forward only when the door is ready, and release wrapped, labelled pallets staged in Zone D for loading and sealing.

10. The maintenance technician maintains trucks, racking and dock equipment, including levellers, racking, wrappers and the baler. Every repair is logged, defects reported by floor staff are actioned or made safe without delay, and the monthly documented racking inspection and daily truck checks are supported and recorded.

11. The 2 floaters cover absence and peak workload across inbound, picking, packing and dispatch as directed by the shift supervisor. They work only to tasks they are trained and, for trucks, authorised for, and they follow the same zone discipline, PPE, scanner and handover rules as the teams they support.

title: Approvals and Sign-offs
text:
1. Approvals on site are fixed by role and no one approves outside their authority. The warehouse manager holds final sign-offs for the site, the shift supervisor holds shift-level approvals, and the dispatcher holds dock and load-release authority. Where a matter needs a higher approval, floor staff escalate it through the shift supervisor to the manager.

2. Damaged-goods write-offs are split by value. The shift supervisor on duty approves write-offs up to and including 500 EUR once the goods have been quarantined in Zone F and inspected. Any write-off above 500 EUR is reserved to the warehouse manager and is not posted without the manager's signature.

3. Damaged goods move to quarantine in Zone F on the same day they are found, under PR-09. Returns staff and stock controllers identify and record the damage, the supervisor or manager approves the write-off within their limit, and only then is the system adjustment posted. No damaged stock is scrapped, reworked or returned to sale without that approval.

4. Returns decisions follow a propose-and-approve rule. Returns and packing staff in Zone F accept returns only within 14 days of delivery, inspect every unit, and propose restock, rework or scrap for each line under PR-07. The final disposition is approved only by the shift supervisor, who confirms the inspection result before goods re-enter Zone B, Zone E, or scrap.

5. Stock accuracy approvals belong to stock control and management. No inventory adjustment is ever posted without a second count, and recounts and adjustments prepared by the stock controllers require approval before booking. The annual wall-to-wall stocktake is worked under stock control and is personally signed off by the warehouse manager before it is closed.

6. Overtime is a manager-only approval. Only the warehouse manager approves overtime, including peak-season Saturday morning working. Shift supervisors may identify the need and roster floaters within the shift, but they do not authorise additional hours, additional shifts or extended opening on their own authority.

7. Dock scheduling is owned by the dispatcher. The dispatcher books transport, assigns every carrier a specific door and time slot, and resolves conflicts over door use. Inbound Doors 1-4 and outbound Doors 5-8 are assigned strictly by flow, drivers wait in the marked waiting area until called, and no vehicle approaches a dock without dispatcher confirmation.

8. Outbound release is also a dispatcher authority. Only wrapped, labelled pallets staged in Zone D for a specific load are released, and the truck is loaded and sealed only on dispatcher instruction under PR-06. The shift supervisor directs staging and labour priorities, but does not override the door assignment or release.

9. Two further approvals are reserved. Only the warehouse manager authorises new forklift operators, and no licence means no truck, and the shift supervisor reviews every incident report arising on the shift before it is closed or escalated to the manager. Repairs, racking inspections and daily truck checks are logged by maintenance but do not replace these sign-offs.

title: Dock Booking and Arrival
text:
1. All inbound deliveries arrive only through Doors 1-4, which are designated inbound only. No inbound unloading takes place at outbound Doors 5-8, and no inbound vehicle is reassigned to an outbound door to clear a backlog. The dispatcher owns dock scheduling for all inbound and outbound movements and resolves any conflict over door use.

2. Every inbound delivery is booked in advance with a specific date, door number and time slot. The dispatcher books transport, confirms the carrier, vehicle type, purchase order or delivery reference, and pallet quantity, and assigns the door and slot before the vehicle travels. No carrier approaches a dock without dispatcher confirmation of door and slot.

3. Inbound slots are planned inside the two operating shifts, Monday to Friday, mornings 06:00-14:00 and afternoons 14:00-22:00. In peak season, Saturday morning overtime slots may be added, but only where approved by the warehouse manager. The dispatcher sequences arrivals to keep Zone A receiving clear and to avoid queuing onto public roads.

4. On arrival at the site, drivers report first to the office annex driver reception and never drive directly to a dock. The dispatcher or inbound team verifies the booking, identity, door number and slot, and issues waiting instructions. Drivers and visitors do not enter the operational floor unless specifically authorised and escorted.

5. After check-in, drivers wait with their vehicle in the marked waiting area in the fenced yard until called forward. Waiting in the hall, on dock approaches, in manoeuvring lanes or at a door without instruction is prohibited. Unscheduled, early or late vehicles hold in the yard or waiting area until the dispatcher gives a revised door and slot.

6. Vehicles are called forward only when the assigned Door 1-4, its leveller, and the Zone A receiving team are ready. The dispatcher confirms the door number a second time at call-forward, and the driver proceeds by the marked manoeuvring lane to the assigned door. Drivers follow yard traffic markings at all times and give way at pedestrian crossings and dock ramps.

7. Speed limits apply to every vehicle movement on arrival. The limit is 15 km/h in the yard and 5 km/h in all shared areas, including pedestrian zones, crossings and the dock ramps and approaches. Reversing to the dock is done slowly, on mirrors and, where provided, with guidance from the inbound team, and the vehicle is braked, switched off and secured before dock work begins.

8. At the dock, the driver presents the delivery documents for checking and remains in the designated safe position during unloading. Nothing is unloaded until the documents have been checked in line with PR-01. Each dock door has its own leveller, which is positioned only by trained staff, and any defect to a door, leveller or seal is reported immediately to maintenance and the dispatcher.

9. Early, late or non-compliant arrivals are managed by the dispatcher in consultation with the shift supervisor in charge of the floor. The dispatcher may re-time, reassign to another inbound door, or hold the vehicle, and updates Zone A priorities accordingly. The outcome, revised door and slot, and any refusal or delay are recorded and carried into the end-of-shift handover.

title: Checking and Inspection
text:
1. No vehicle is unloaded until its delivery documents have been checked in Zone A. The inbound operator compares the delivery note, purchase order or delivery reference, supplier, product descriptions, quantities, batch or expiry data where applicable, and the booked door and time slot. Any mismatch stops the process before unloading begins.

2. If documents are missing, incorrect or do not match the booking, the inbound team holds the vehicle at the door and escalates to the shift supervisor and dispatcher. Nothing moves past Zone A until the paperwork is resolved. The vehicle waits in place or is returned to the waiting area, and the decision and delay are recorded for handover.

3. Once documents are accepted, unloading takes place only at the assigned Door 1-4 using the door leveller positioned by trained staff. Inbound operators unload with electric or hand pallet jacks or by forklift where required, placing all pallets and cartons inside the marked Zone A receiving area. Drivers remain in the designated safe position and do not enter the handling area.

4. Every delivery is counted in Zone A against the checked documents. Inbound operators count pallets, cartons and units as applicable, confirm quantities by purchase order line, and record overages, shortages and part-pallets immediately. The count is the basis for booking and no estimate or unchecked quantity is passed forward.

5. Every delivery is inspected in Zone A after unloading and counting. Inbound operators check outer packaging integrity, labelling, pallet condition and stability, visible damage, leakage or contamination, and, for chilled or hazmat lines, correct identification and segregation. Inspection applies to the full delivery, not to a sample.

6. Only inspected goods are booked into the system, and only booked goods go to put-away in Zone B, E or F. System booking records the accepted quantity by product, quantity, batch and location instruction, and references the checked documents. Uninspected, uncounted or unbooked goods never leave Zone A and are never picked, packed or dispatched.

7. Goods that require special storage are identified at inspection and kept segregated in Zone A until put-away. Chilled goods requiring the +2 °C to +8 °C regime are prioritised for immediate transfer to Zone E. Hazardous goods are identified for the ventilated hazmat cage in Zone F and never mixed with general stock. Damaged or suspect goods are separated at once.

8. Damaged goods found during inbound inspection go to quarantine in Zone F on the same day they are found under PR-09. Inbound operators label and segregate the affected pallets or cartons, record the damage with the delivery reference and photographs where required, and notify the shift supervisor and stock control. No damaged line is booked as available stock.

9. Returns and refusals at inbound are not mixed with clean receipts. Any delivery or part-delivery rejected for document failure, damage, temperature failure or non-compliance is held separately in Zone A, recorded, and dealt with only on instruction from the shift supervisor and dispatcher. The carrier is not released until the outcome is confirmed.

10. On completion, Zone A is cleared by flow. Accepted, booked pallets are released for put-away to Zone B, E or F, quarantine lines are transferred to Zone F, and the receiving bay is left clear for the next booked slot. All counts, inspection results, bookings and exceptions are entered before the next vehicle is called forward and carried into the shift record.

title: Booking and Release
text:
1. Only inspected goods are booked into the system, and only booked goods are released for put-away. Booking is the formal transfer from receiving in Zone A to storage in Zone B, Zone E or Zone F under PR-01, and put-away from that point follows PR-02. Nothing leaves Zone A without a system booking.

2. Booking takes place in Zone A immediately after counting and inspection are complete and the delivery documents have been accepted. Inbound operators enter the accepted quantity using the handheld WMS scanners, working from the checked delivery note and purchase order reference. No estimate, uncounted quantity or uninspected pallet is booked.

3. Each booking records product identity, accepted quantity by purchase order line, batch and expiry data where applicable, pallet identity and condition, and the checked document reference. Overages, shortages, part-pallets and rejected lines are recorded as exceptions at the time of booking and are not added to available stock. The system stock is therefore the stock on the rack.

4. On booking, the system directs the put-away destination. General ambient packed goods are directed to bulk storage in Zone B, chilled goods requiring +2 °C to +8 °C are directed to Zone E, and hazardous goods are directed to the ventilated hazmat cage in Zone F. Inbound operators do not choose an alternative location or bypass the directed location.

5. Every booked pallet is labelled before release. Labels carry product, quantity, batch, booking reference and directed storage location, and are fixed so they remain readable for scanning at put-away. A pallet without a booking label stays in Zone A and is not offered for put-away.

6. Release to put-away is by booked load only. Once labelled, booked pallets are staged by destination within the marked Zone A release area, kept clear of the dock leveller, aisles and the next receiving bay, and handed over to forklift operators for movement to Zone B, E or F. Unbooked, unlabeled or quarantined goods are never included in a release.

7. Time-critical lines are released first. Booked chilled goods are released for immediate transfer to Zone E without waiting for the full delivery to be booked, and booked hazmat lines are released directly to the cage in Zone F. In both cases booking and labelling still come first, and segregation is maintained through the move.

8. Exceptions are never released to storage. Damaged or suspect goods go to quarantine in Zone F on the same day they are found under PR-09 and are booked only as quarantine, not as available stock. Document failures, rejected deliveries and quantity disputes remain held separately in Zone A until resolved on instruction from the shift supervisor and dispatcher.

9. Zone A is cleared by booking. A receiving bay is closed only when all accepted lines are booked and released, all quarantine lines are transferred to Zone F, and all counts, inspection results, bookings and exceptions are entered in the system and in the shift record. The next vehicle is called forward to Doors 1-4 only when the bay is clear, and any open exception is carried into the end-of-shift handover.

title: Storage Limits and Layout
text:
1. Zone B — bulk storage occupies 2,200 m2 of the hall and is the only area for general ambient bulk stock. It contains high-bay pallet racking providing 2,400 pallet positions, plus defined block-stack areas for overflow where racking is not used. No bulk stock is held outside Zone B except chilled goods in Zone E and hazardous goods in the cage in Zone F.

2. The governing unit for all storage capacity is the full-weight pallet of 1,000 kg, load included. No pallet, load included, may weigh more than 1,000 kg anywhere on site. Racking loads, bay loads, forklift and reach-truck ratings, and transport limits are all built on this figure.

3. Each rack bay in Zone B carries at most 2,700 kg in total. The bay limit applies to the combined weight of all pallets, packaging and load on that bay at any time, and it is never exceeded even where individual pallets are below 1,000 kg. Stock controllers and forklift operators check weight by system data and label before put-away.

4. Pallets are placed only in their directed rack position and only by reach truck or forklift rated for the weight and height. The 4 reach trucks rated at 1.6 t serve the high bays and the 6 counterbalance forklifts rated at 2.5 t serve general work. Overweight, damaged or unstable pallets are not put into racking and are reported to the shift supervisor.

5. Where goods are block-stacked outside the racking, stacks are limited to 3 pallets high and to 4.0 m in total height, including pallet and load. Both limits apply together, so a stack stops at whichever limit is reached first. No free stacking above 4.0 m takes place anywhere, even though the hall provides 10 m clear height.

6. Block stacks stand only in marked block-stack areas inside Zone B. They are built square, stable and uniformly bonded, with the heaviest pallets at the bottom and lighter pallets above. Leaning, overhanging or mixed-footprint stacks are broken down and rebuilt before they are booked as stored.

7. Rack storage aisles in Zone B are 3.0 m wide. Main transport aisles through and around Zone B are 4.0 m wide. Aisle widths are marked on the floor and are kept clear at all times for truck manoeuvre and visibility. Nothing is stored, staged or parked in an aisle, across a rack face, or in a way that blocks a leveller, emergency exit or pedestrian route.

8. Pedestrian walkways adjoining Zone B are physically separated by yellow barriers and are 1.2 m wide. Pedestrians in and around bulk storage use only these walkways and the marked crossings. Forklift operators give way at every crossing and observe the 5 km/h limit in all shared areas.

9. Zone discipline applies to every pallet in bulk storage. Only inspected and booked goods directed under PR-02 are put away to Zone B, and every pallet carries its booking label with product, quantity, batch and location. Unbooked goods from Zone A, unwrapped or unlabelled pallets for Zone D, quarantined goods, chilled goods and hazmat are never placed in bulk racking or block stacks.

10. Any damage, overload or instability found in Zone B is made safe immediately and reported to the shift supervisor and maintenance technician. Damaged goods go to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found, and damaged or suspect racking is offloaded and barriered until repaired. Racking remains in service only within its documented bay, weight, height and aisle limits.

title: Put-away to Storage
text:
1. Put-away moves only booked goods from Zone A receiving to storage under PR-02. No pallet leaves Zone A without system booking, booking label and directed location. Uninspected, uncounted, unbooked or quarantine goods are never put away.

2. The system directs every put-away destination at booking. General ambient packed goods are directed to bulk storage in Zone B, chilled goods are directed to Zone E, and hazardous goods are directed to the ventilated hazmat cage in Zone F. Forklift operators do not choose an alternative location or bypass the directed bay or position.

3. Booked pallets are handed over in the marked Zone A release area by destination. Forklift operators collect only labelled pallets staged for put-away, verify product, quantity and directed location against the label, and scan the pallet with a handheld WMS scanner before moving. A pallet without a readable label stays in Zone A.

4. All movements to racking and block stacks are made by authorised equipment only. The 4 reach trucks rated at 1.6 t serve the high bays in Zone B and the 6 counterbalance forklifts rated at 2.5 t serve general put-away and block stacking. No other staff drive forklifts or reach trucks, and only the warehouse manager authorises new operators.

5. At the rack face the operator confirms the location before placing. The pallet label and system task are scanned, the bay number and level are checked, and the bay weight is respected. Each rack bay carries at most 2,700 kg in total, built on the 1,000 kg maximum per pallet load included. An overweight, damaged or unstable pallet is not placed in racking.

6. Block put-away outside the racking follows the same scan control. Stacks stand only in marked block-stack areas inside Zone B, limited to 3 pallets high and 4.0 m total height together. Heaviest pallets go at the bottom, stacks are built square and stable, and leaning or overhanging stacks are rebuilt before booking as stored.

7. Time-critical lines are put away first. Booked chilled goods go immediately to Zone E to protect the +2 °C to +8 °C regime, and booked hazmat lines go directly to the cage in Zone F without staging elsewhere. Segregation is maintained through the whole move, and hazmat never sits outside the cage.

8. Every placement is scan-confirmed at the storage position. The operator scans the pallet and the location, and only a system-confirmed placement counts as stored. If the location is occupied, damaged, or does not match the task, the pallet is held clear of the aisle and the problem is reported to the shift supervisor and stock control.

9. Aisles and walkways are kept clear through put-away. Rack storage aisles of 3.0 m and main transport aisles of 4.0 m are never blocked by standing pallets, and pedestrian walkways of 1.2 m behind yellow barriers are used by all pedestrians. Operators observe 10 km/h inside the hall and 5 km/h at crossings, pedestrian zones and ramps.

10. Zone A is cleared and Zone B discipline is closed by task. On completion the operator returns empty pallets and wrapping to their points, Zone A release bays are left clear for the next booking, and any held, rejected or damaged pallet is transferred to quarantine in Zone F the same day. All put-away confirmations and exceptions are in the system before handover.

title: Racking Inspections
text:
1. All high-bay pallet racking in Zone B is subject to a documented safety inspection every month. The inspection covers every in-service rack bay, its uprights, beams, bracing, base plates and floor fixings, load notices, location labels, and the condition of pallets and loads upon it. No rack remains in use without passing within the monthly cycle.

2. The maintenance technician owns the inspection programme and its records. The technician plans the monthly round so that all 2,400 pallet positions in the 2,200 m2 bulk store are checked, carries out or supervises the check, logs every defect and every repair, and files the signed monthly report for review. Defects that cannot be repaired immediately are made safe the same day.

3. Stock controllers and shift supervisors support the check from daily operation. They report any impact, scrape, lean, overload, instability, missing beam lock, damaged pallet, or obscured label to the maintenance technician and the shift supervisor on duty at once. A reported suspect bay is not used for put-away or picking until it has been inspected and cleared.

4. Each inspection verifies load discipline bay by bay. Each rack bay carries at most 2,700 kg in total, built on the site maximum of 1,000 kg per pallet load included. The inspector checks system weights against bay labels, looks for overhanging, crushed or leaning pallets, and confirms that overweight, damaged or unstable pallets have not been placed in racking.

5. Each inspection verifies structural and layout discipline. Rack storage aisles are 3.0 m wide and main transport aisles are 4.0 m wide, marked and kept clear. Pedestrian walkways of 1.2 m behind yellow barriers are intact and unobstructed. Uprights are vertical, beams are level and locked, bracing and anchors are secure, and no goods, pallets or equipment are stored against racking or in aisles.

6. Block-stack areas are checked in the same round. Stacks stand only in marked areas inside Zone B, limited to 3 pallets high and 4.0 m total height together, built square and stable with the heaviest pallets at the bottom. Leaning, overhanging or mixed-footprint stacks are broken down and rebuilt before they are booked as stored.

7. Any damaged or suspect racking is taken out of service immediately. The bay is offloaded if safe to do so, barriered and labelled out of use, and reported to the shift supervisor and the maintenance technician. No pallet is placed into, and no pick is made from, a barriered bay. The barrier remains until repair and re-inspection are signed off.

8. Damaged goods found during the inspection go to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found under PR-09. The affected pallet is labelled, segregated, scan-recorded and transferred, and stock control investigates any system discrepancy. No damaged stock is returned to racking and no adjustment is posted without a second count.

9. Every inspection, defect, offload, barriering, repair and return to service is documented. The monthly report records date, inspector, bays checked, defects found, immediate safeguards, repairs completed, parts replaced, and bays still out of service. Repair logs are kept with the report, and open items are carried into the end-of-shift handover until closed.

10. The shift supervisor on duty reviews every racking incident report on the shift before it is closed or escalated to the warehouse manager. Impacts from trucks, falling goods, dock equipment faults and any injury or near miss are reported as incidents, the scene is preserved for review, and follow-up put-away respects the 10 km/h hall limit and the 5 km/h limit at crossings, pedestrian zones and ramps.

title: Cold Zone Handling
text:
1. Zone E — cold zone is the enclosed 300 m2 chilled store inside the hall for temperature-sensitive packed goods. It is held continuously between +2 °C and +8 °C. No other zone is used for chilled storage, and no ambient, quarantine or hazardous goods are placed in Zone E.

2. Only inspected and booked chilled goods are put away to Zone E under PR-12. Identification starts in Zone A at inspection, booking directs the destination as Zone E, and segregation is maintained through release and put-away. Uninspected, uncounted or unbooked goods never enter Zone E.

3. Booked chilled lines are prioritised for immediate transfer. They are released first from the Zone A release area and moved directly to Zone E without waiting for the full delivery to be booked and without staging in Zone B, Zone C or Zone D. Forklift operators maintain segregation and keep doors and transit time to a minimum.

4. The cold store is fitted with continuous temperature monitoring and alarms. Alarms signal any excursion outside +2 °C to +8 °C, door left open, or equipment fault. On alarm the shift supervisor is notified at once, secures the stock, calls the maintenance technician, and preserves the temperature record for review.

5. A manual temperature verification is carried out in Zone E on every shift, mornings 06:00-14:00 and afternoons 14:00-22:00. The check uses the calibrated display and manual thermometer at the defined points, is recorded with date, time, reading and checker name, and is reviewed in the end-of-shift handover under PR-15.

6. Doors, seals and curtains to Zone E are kept closed except for active put-away, replenishment or picking moves. Staff enter only for a directed task, wear high-visibility vests and class S3 footwear as on the rest of the floor, and observe the 10 km/h hall limit and 5 km/h at pedestrian zones, crossings and ramps on approach to the cold doors.

7. Every placement and pick in Zone E is scan-confirmed with the handheld WMS scanners. Pallets carry their booking label with product, quantity, batch, expiry and location, respect the 1,000 kg maximum per pallet load included, and are placed only in their directed position. Block stacks, where used, respect 3 pallets high and 4.0 m together.

8. Cold-chain discipline applies to every movement in and out. Pick faces in Zone C fed from Zone E are replenished before each picking shift and returned promptly, picked chilled goods move to Zone D only after scan-verification, packing and labelling, and chilled returns move only through Zone F inspection. Chilled stock is never left standing in aisles, Zone A or Zone D.

9. Any temperature excursion, damaged packaging, leakage or suspect cold-chain break is treated as damaged goods under PR-09. The affected pallets are labelled, segregated and moved to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found, recorded with batch and temperature data, and notified to the shift supervisor and stock control. No affected line is booked or dispatched as available stock.

10. All cold-zone records are kept in the shift record. Automatic logs, manual shift verifications, alarm events, put-away and pick confirmations, quarantine transfers and maintenance actions are entered before handover, and open faults or quarantined batches are carried forward until closed. The monthly racking inspection includes Zone E racking, and no faulty bay or door remains in service without barriering and repair logging.

title: Hazmat Cage Limits
text:
1. All hazardous goods on site are stored only in the separate ventilated hazmat cage inside Zone F. The cage provides 60 m2 of dedicated, ventilated floor within the 600 m2 services and control area. No hazardous goods are stored anywhere else on site, not in Zone A, Zone B, Zone C, Zone D, Zone E, or elsewhere in Zone F.

2. The total quantity in the cage never exceeds 4,000 kg at any one time. The limit applies to the combined weight of all goods, packaging, pallets and load held in the cage together, including booked stock, stock awaiting inspection decision, and any quarantined hazmat line.

3. The governing unit is the full-weight pallet of 1,000 kg, load included. No pallet, load included, may weigh more than 1,000 kg. The 4,000 kg cage limit therefore means at most 4 full-weight pallets in the cage at any one time, and fewer where pallets are part-weight but other lines bring the total to the limit.

4. Identification starts in Zone A under PR-01 and PR-13. Inbound operators identify hazmat lines at document check and inspection, keep them segregated in the marked Zone A receiving area, and never mix them with general, chilled or damaged stock. Booking directs the destination as the hazmat cage, and the pallet carries its booking label with product, quantity, hazard data and directed location.

5. Booked hazmat lines move directly to the cage without staging elsewhere. They are released first from the Zone A release area, moved by authorised forklift operators with WMS scan confirmation, and placed only in their directed position in the cage. They are never staged in Zone B block stacks or racking, in Zone C pick faces, or in Zone D dispatch staging.

6. Separation is maintained inside and outside the cage. Incompatible hazard classes are kept apart to instruction and never stacked together, leaking or damaged containers are segregated at once, and the cage is kept clear of general packing materials, returns, quarantine ambient goods and waste. The 4.0 m main transport aisle and adjoining pedestrian walkways of 1.2 m behind yellow barriers are kept clear at all times.

7. Access to the cage is controlled. Staff enter only for a directed put-away, count, pick or inspection task under PR-13, wear high-visibility vests and class S3 safety footwear as on the rest of the floor, and observe the 10 km/h hall limit and 5 km/h at pedestrian zones, crossings and ramps. Unauthorised staff, drivers and visitors never enter.

8. Every placement, move and removal is scan-confirmed with the handheld WMS scanners. Stock controllers own the cage quantity day to day, verify the 4,000 kg total before any new put-away is accepted, and refuse any booking that would exceed the limit. No adjustment is posted without a second count, and over-limit or unbooked pallets are held in Zone A until space is confirmed.

9. Spill response follows PR-13 at all times. Spill kits, extinguishers and safety data sheets for the stored classes are kept at the cage entrance and checked each shift. On any leak, spill or alarm the shift supervisor is notified at once, the area is secured and ventilated, the maintenance technician is called, and the incident is recorded for review. Contaminated goods go to quarantine within Zone F the same day they are found and are not returned to sale without supervisor approval.

10. The cage, its ventilation, racking, bunding, signage and load notices are included in the monthly documented racking inspection, with every defect and repair logged by the maintenance technician. Damaged or suspect racking is offloaded, barriered and kept out of service until repaired. All cage holdings, checks, spills and quarantine transfers are entered in the shift record and carried into the end-of-shift handover under PR-15 until closed.

title: Replenishment of Pick Faces
text:
1. Zone C pick faces and flow racks are fed only from bulk storage under PR-03. Replenishment moves inspected and booked stock from Zone B, and for chilled lines from Zone E, to the ground-level pick faces in Zone C. Nothing is replenished from Zone A, Zone D, Zone F quarantine or the hazmat cage.

2. Replenishment is completed before each picking shift starts. The morning 06:00-14:00 faces are filled before morning picking begins, and the afternoon 14:00-22:00 faces are filled before afternoon picking begins. Pickers work only from replenished, system-directed faces and never pick from bulk racking or unbooked stock.

3. The system directs every replenishment task. Using the 20 handheld WMS scanners, forklift operators and stock controllers work from scanner tasks showing source location in bulk, product, quantity, batch and destination pick face. No manual top-up, alternative source or alternative face is used outside the task.

4. Only authorised forklift operators move replenishment pallets. The 4 reach trucks rated at 1.6 t serve the high bays in Zone B and the 6 counterbalance forklifts rated at 2.5 t serve general moves, with the 8 electric and 12 hand pallet jacks for small top-ups. No other staff drive forklifts or reach trucks.

5. At the source bay the operator scan-confirms the pallet and location before lifting. Each rack bay carries at most 2,700 kg in total, built on the site maximum of 1,000 kg per pallet load included. Overweight, damaged, unstable or unlabelled pallets are not used for replenishment and are reported to the shift supervisor.

6. At the pick face the operator scan-confirms placement. Pallets, cartons and flow-rack loads are placed only in their directed face, with labels facing out, within weight and height discipline, and without overfilling the face or blocking the adjacent rack storage aisle. Block top-ups respect 3 pallets high and 4.0 m together.

7. Time-critical lines are replenished first. Chilled faces fed from Zone E are replenished with immediate return to keep the +2 °C to +8 °C regime, with doors and transit time kept to a minimum. Hazmat lines, where picked, are replenished only to their directed segregated face and never mixed with general stock.

8. Aisles, walkways and faces are kept clear through replenishment. Rack storage aisles of 3.0 m and main transport aisles of 4.0 m are never blocked by standing pallets, and pedestrian walkways of 1.2 m behind yellow barriers are used by all pedestrians. Operators observe 10 km/h inside the hall and 5 km/h at crossings, pedestrian zones and ramps.

9. Every replenishment move is scan-recorded before picking is released. The system stock is the stock on the rack, so only a system-confirmed placement counts as available to pick. If the source is empty, short or damaged, the operator holds clear of the aisle and reports to stock control and the shift supervisor for a recount or alternative source.

10. Damaged goods found during replenishment go to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found under PR-09. The face is not filled from a damaged pallet, the damage is recorded with product, batch and location, and no adjustment is posted without a second count. All tasks, confirmations and exceptions are in the system before the picking shift starts and are carried into handover.

title: Scanner Order Picking
text:
1. Order picking takes place only in Zone C under PR-04 and only from replenished pick faces and flow racks. Pickers work against system scanner tasks on the 20 shared handheld WMS scanners and pick only from the directed face shown on the task. Picking from bulk racking in Zone B, from Zone A, from quarantine in Zone F, or from unbooked stock is prohibited.

2. Picking starts only after replenishment for the shift is system-confirmed. The morning 06:00-14:00 orders are picked from faces replenished before morning picking, and the afternoon 14:00-22:00 orders are picked from faces replenished before afternoon picking. If a face is empty, short or damaged, the picker holds the task and reports to the shift supervisor and stock control.

3. Each picker works one scanner task at a time in task sequence. The scanner directs the pick face, product, batch and expiry where applicable, quantity and container. Pickers follow the scanner route through the ground-level faces, keep the 3.0 m rack storage aisles and 4.0 m main aisles clear, and use only the 1.2 m walkways behind yellow barriers on foot.

4. Every picked item is scan-verified before it is packed. The picker scans the source face and then scans each item or carton as picked, confirming product, quantity and batch against the task. No item leaves its face without a scan, and any scan mismatch stops the pick until stock control recounts and corrects the task.

5. Pickers check condition as they pick. Outer packaging, labelling, seal, date and stability are checked at the face, and chilled lines for the +2 °C to +8 °C regime and segregated hazmat lines are kept apart and moved without delay. Damaged, leaking or suspect units are not picked to order.

6. Damaged goods found at the pick face go to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found under PR-09. The picker segregates the affected units, records product, batch and face location, notifies the shift supervisor and stock control, and does not complete the order line from damaged stock. No adjustment is posted without a second count.

7. Picked quantities respect the site weight discipline. No pallet, load included, may weigh more than 1,000 kg, and pick pallets and cartons are built stable, square and within face height limits. Overweight, unstable or overhanging picks are rebuilt before they leave Zone C.

8. After scan-verification the picker packs, labels and separates the order by destination. Packed cartons and pallets carry order, product, quantity and batch identification, remain in their assigned Zone C flow, and are handed over only for transfer to dispatch. Only wrapped, labelled pallets move to Zone D.

9. Pickers remain under the shift supervisor in charge of the floor for tasking and safety. They wear high-visibility vests and class S3 safety footwear at all times on the floor, give way to trucks at every crossing, and observe pedestrian rules in full. Electric and hand pallet jacks for small moves in Zone C are used only by trained staff.

10. Every task is scan-closed before the next task is started. Confirmations, shortages, batch substitutions and exceptions are recorded on the scanner at the face and appear in the system before handover. Open picks, short faces and quarantine transfers are carried into the end-of-shift handover under PR-15 and picking for the next shift does not start from unconfirmed stock.

title: Transfer to Dispatch
text:
1. Transfer to dispatch moves only scan-verified picks from Zone C toward Zone D under PR-04 and PR-05. No carton or pallet leaves the pick face without scanner confirmation of product, quantity and batch, and no unpicked, unverified or damaged stock is transferred.

2. After scan-verification, goods are packed and labelled in the Zone C to Zone D flow. Packers confirm order identity, quantity, batch and expiry where applicable, apply the correct customer and handling labels, and build pallets stable, square and readable for scanning. No pallet, load included, may weigh more than 1,000 kg.

3. Labelled pallets are handed over for movement to Zone D by destination and outbound door. Forklift operators and trained pallet-jack operators collect only packed, labelled units, scan the pallet with the handheld WMS scanners before moving, and keep chilled lines for the +2 °C to +8 °C regime and segregated hazmat lines apart and without delay.

4. All transfer moves use authorised equipment only. The 6 counterbalance forklifts rated at 2.5 t serve general transfer work, with the 8 electric and 12 hand pallet jacks for small moves. Reach trucks rated at 1.6 t remain on high-bay work and are not used for dispatch running. No other staff drive forklifts or reach trucks.

5. Only wrapped, labelled pallets are staged in Zone D. Pallets arriving from Zone C are wrapped on the 2 semi-automatic stretch wrappers, checked for wrap integrity, label readability and stability, and then placed in the marked staging lane for their assigned outbound Door 5-8 and load. Unwrapped, unlabelled or unbooked pallets never enter Zone D.

6. Staging in Zone D is by door and load under dispatcher control. Pallets stand only in their directed lane, kept clear of levellers, main transport aisles of 4.0 m, rack storage aisles of 3.0 m, pedestrian walkways of 1.2 m behind yellow barriers, and emergency exits. Nothing is double-staged, restacked or held in an aisle to clear Zone C.

7. The dispatcher owns release from Zone D under PR-06. Staged pallets wait for dispatcher release before loading, and trucks at Doors 5-8 are loaded and sealed only on dispatcher instruction. The shift supervisor sets transfer and staging priorities and redeploys pickers, packers and floaters, but does not override the door assignment or release.

8. Zone C faces and transfer lanes are cleared by flow. On completion, operators return empty pallets and waste to their points, leave pick faces tidy and replenishable for the next shift, and leave Zone D lanes countable for dispatch. Open picks, short orders and waiting pallets are recorded in the system before handover.

9. Safety and PPE rules apply through every transfer. All staff wear high-visibility vests and class S3 safety footwear on the floor, operators wear seat belts whenever the truck is moving, and all moves observe 10 km/h inside the hall and 5 km/h at pedestrian zones, crossings and dock ramps. Pedestrians use only marked walkways and crossings.

10. Damaged goods found during packing, wrapping or transfer go to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found under PR-09. The affected units are segregated, labelled and scan-recorded with order and batch reference, notified to the shift supervisor and stock control, and never staged in Zone D. All transfers, wraps, staging confirmations and exceptions are in the system and carried into the end-of-shift handover under PR-15.

title: Packing and Wrapping
text:
1. Packing and wrapping covers all standard outbound packing after scan-verified picking under PR-05. Picked items move from the Zone C pick faces through packing and labelling, then wrapping, and only wrapped, labelled pallets move to Zone D. Unverified, unpacked or damaged goods are never packed for dispatch.

2. Packing starts only after every picked item has been scan-verified at the face. Using the handheld WMS scanners, packers confirm order identity, customer, product, quantity, batch and expiry where applicable against the scanner task. Any scan mismatch, short pick or suspect unit stops the pack until stock control and the shift supervisor resolve it.

3. Packers build each carton and pallet stable, square and countable. Heavy items go at the bottom, lighter items above, with no overhang, leaning or mixed-footprint build. No pallet, load included, may weigh more than 1,000 kg, and any build approaching that weight is weighed or checked by system data and broken down before wrapping.

4. Every packed unit is labelled before it leaves the packing flow. Labels carry order, product, quantity, batch, handling marks and directed outbound door and load, and are fixed flat and readable for scanning at staging and loading. A pallet without a correct, readable label stays in the Zone C to Zone D flow and never enters Zone D.

5. Chilled lines for the +2 °C to +8 °C regime and segregated hazmat lines are packed and labelled apart and without delay. They are kept in their directed flow, not mixed with general ambient packs, and chilled packs are not left standing in ambient aisles. Any temperature, leakage or damage suspicion sends the units to quarantine instead of wrap.

6. Wrapping is done on the 2 semi-automatic stretch wrappers serving the dispatch flow. Operators wrap only packed, labelled pallets, centre the pallet on the turntable, secure the tail, and wrap to full stability with base and top coverage. Wrap integrity, edge protection and label readability through or outside the film are checked on every pallet.

7. A pallet is accepted for Zone D only when it is fully wrapped, stable and labelled. Unwrapped, part-wrapped, unstable, overhanging or overweight pallets are rejected at the wrapper, unwrapped where safe, rebuilt and re-wrapped. Rejected wrapping film and damaged cartons are cleared to waste and the cardboard baler point, never left in the packing lanes.

8. Packing and wrapping work stays inside its marked lanes between Zone C and Zone D. Main transport aisles of 4.0 m, rack storage aisles of 3.0 m, pedestrian walkways of 1.2 m behind yellow barriers and access to the wrappers and levellers are kept clear at all times. Empty pallets, film reels and waste are returned to their points during the shift.

9. Value-added packing tasks, such as reboxing, kitting or display builds, take place only in Zone F to instruction and are handed back into the standard flow for scan-verification, labelling and wrapping. Returns and packing staff do not release value-added packs directly to Zone D without confirmation and labels.

10. All staff wear high-visibility vests and class S3 safety footwear in the packing and wrapping areas, operators wear seat belts whenever the truck is moving, and all moves observe 10 km/h inside the hall and 5 km/h at pedestrian zones, crossings and dock ramps. Damaged goods found during packing or wrapping go to quarantine in Zone F the same day under PR-09, and all packs, wraps and exceptions are scan-recorded in the system before handover under PR-15.

title: Staging and Loading
text:
1. Staging and loading take place only in Zone D in front of outbound Doors 5-8 under PR-06. Doors 5-8 are outbound only, and no inbound unloading takes place at these doors. Only wrapped, labelled pallets released for a specific outbound load are staged here.

2. Pallets enter Zone D only after packing and wrapping are complete. Every pallet is fully stretch-wrapped on the semi-automatic wrappers, stable and square, with a correct, readable label showing order, product, quantity, batch and directed door and load. Unwrapped, part-wrapped, unstable or unlabelled pallets never enter Zone D.

3. Staging is by door and load under dispatcher control. Pallets stand only in their directed marked lane for their assigned Door 5-8 and load, sequenced for loading order. Nothing is double-staged, restacked in the lane, or held in an aisle to clear Zone C.

4. Zone D lanes are kept clear and countable at all times. Main transport aisles of 4.0 m, rack storage aisles of 3.0 m and pedestrian walkways of 1.2 m behind yellow barriers are never blocked by standing pallets. Access to levellers, emergency exits, fire equipment and pedestrian crossings is kept free.

5. Outbound vehicles arrive only on dispatcher instruction. The dispatcher books transport, assigns every carrier a specific outbound door and time slot, and calls vehicles forward from the marked waiting area only when the door, leveller and staged load are ready. Drivers report to the office annex on arrival and wait in the yard waiting area, never in the hall.

6. At the dock, the vehicle is positioned, braked, switched off and secured before loading begins. Each Door 5-8 has its own leveller, positioned only by trained staff. Any defect to a door, leveller or seal is reported immediately to the maintenance technician and the dispatcher, and the door is not used until cleared.

7. Loading starts only on dispatcher release. The dispatcher releases the load by door and reference once all pallets for the load are staged, counted and scan-confirmed in the system. Forklift operators load only released pallets, in release sequence, scanning each pallet with the handheld WMS scanners at staging and at the trailer.

8. Loading respects weight and stability discipline throughout. No pallet, load included, weighs more than 1,000 kg, and pallets are placed square on the trailer bed without overhang, crushing or mixing of segregated chilled and hazmat lines. The operator confirms count and placement against the release, and any short, damaged or mislabelled pallet stops the load until resolved.

9. On completion the load is checked, closed and sealed. The dispatcher or shift supervisor confirms pallet count against the release, checks labels and wrap integrity, closes the trailer doors or curtain, and applies and records the seal number. The truck is released only after sealing, and the seal number and departure time are entered in the system and shift record.

10. Damaged goods found during staging or loading go to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found under PR-09 and are never loaded. All staging, releases, loads, seals and exceptions are scan-recorded before handover under PR-15. Open loads, waiting pallets and delayed vehicles are carried into the end-of-shift handover, with PPE, seat-belt and speed rules — 10 km/h inside, 15 km/h in the yard and 5 km/h at pedestrian zones, crossings and dock ramps — applying to every move.

title: Load and Capacity Rules
text:
1. The governing unit for all outbound capacity is the full-weight pallet of 1,000 kg, load included. No pallet, load included, may weigh more than 1,000 kg anywhere on site, and every trailer, van, door and shift limit in this section is built on that figure.

2. Contracted curtain-side trailers are rated at 24,000 kg total payload on 33 floor pallet positions. Weight governs before floor space, so a trailer takes at most 24 full-weight pallets of 1,000 kg. Floor positions beyond 24 are not used for full-weight pallets and no trailer is loaded above 24,000 kg.

3. The delivery van is rated at 1,200 kg total payload on 6 floor pallet positions. Weight again governs, so the van takes one full-weight pallet of 1,000 kg only. Any consignment heavier than 1,200 kg, or more than one full-weight pallet, goes by trailer and is not split across van trips to avoid the limit.

4. Part-weight pallets are counted by actual system weight, not by floor positions. A trailer may carry more than 24 pallets only where the combined weight including pallets, packaging and load stays at or below 24,000 kg and all pallets stand square on the 33 floor positions without overhang or double-stacking. The dispatcher checks weight before release.

5. Outbound flow is limited by door throughput. Doors 5-8 are outbound only, giving 4 outbound doors per shift. Each door handles 3 trailer loads per shift, including call-forward, dock, load, seal and departure. No door is double-booked and no fourth load per door per shift is promised to a client.

6. The maximum promise per shift is therefore fixed. Four doors at 3 trailer loads each gives 12 trailer loads per shift, and 12 loads at 24 full-weight pallets gives 288 full-weight pallets per shift. This is the most that dispatch can promise a client for one morning 06:00-14:00 or afternoon 14:00-22:00 shift.

7. Planning respects the 288-pallet ceiling in the system. The dispatcher books transport, assigns door and slot, and releases loads under PR-06 only within that ceiling, sequencing staged pallets in Zone D by door and load. Orders above the ceiling roll to the next shift or to approved Saturday morning overtime, which only the warehouse manager approves.

8. Loading discipline enforces the limits at the trailer. Forklift operators load only dispatcher-released pallets in release sequence, scanning each pallet with the handheld WMS scanners at staging and at the trailer. Count and total weight are confirmed against the release before doors are closed and the seal is applied and recorded.

9. Hazmat consignments respect both transport and cage limits together. The ventilated hazmat cage in Zone F holds at most 4,000 kg at any one time, which means at most 4 full-weight pallets in the cage. Hazmat loads are built only from released, segregated cage stock, are never mixed with incompatible classes, and never exceed trailer or van weight limits.

10. Any overweight, unstable, unwrapped or unlabelled pallet is rejected from the load and does not count toward capacity. It is segregated at once, and damaged goods go to quarantine in Zone F the same day under PR-09. All releases, weights, counts, seals and exceptions are scan-recorded in the system before handover under PR-15.

title: Daily Cycle Counts
text:
1. Cycle counts run every working day under PR-08 on a rotating zone schedule. Counting never stops: each working day covers defined bays, faces and lanes in turn so that Zones B, C, E and the hazmat cage in Zone F are all counted in rotation. The rota is planned by the stock controllers and directed by the shift supervisor in charge of the floor.

2. Stock controllers own inventory accuracy day to day. They prepare the daily count tasks, issue them through the handheld WMS scanners, carry out counts and recounts, investigate discrepancies, and prepare adjustments for approval. The system stock is the stock on the rack, so only system-confirmed quantities count as available.

3. Count tasks are worked by location, not by estimate. Each task shows zone, bay or face, product, batch and system quantity. Counters scan the location and then count every pallet, carton and unit in place, checking product identity, batch, expiry where applicable, label readability and pallet condition. Closed, sealed trailers and unbooked goods in Zone A are never included.

4. Counting takes place inside the two shifts, mornings 06:00-14:00 and afternoons 14:00-22:00, without stopping the flow. Counters work in the 3.0 m rack storage aisles and at the ground-level pick faces, keep the 4.0 m main transport aisles clear, and use only the 1.2 m walkways behind yellow barriers on foot. Trucks give way at every crossing.

5. Bulk locations are counted in place. In Zone B each rack bay is counted as found up to its 2,700 kg bay limit, built on the 1,000 kg maximum per pallet load included. Block stacks are counted by marked area within 3 pallets high and 4.0 m together. Overweight, unstable or unlabelled pallets are reported and not counted as correct until resolved.

6. Pick faces, cold store and hazmat cage follow the same rota with segregation kept. Zone C faces are counted after replenishment is confirmed, Zone E chilled stock is counted without breaking the +2 °C to +8 °C regime, and hazmat lines are counted only in the ventilated 60 m2 cage under its 4,000 kg limit. Incompatible classes are never moved together to count.

7. No inventory adjustment is ever posted without a second count. Where the first count differs from the system, a different checker recounts the same location blind, without seeing the first result. Only two matching counts, or a supervised investigation that explains the difference, allow an adjustment to be proposed.

8. Damaged or suspect stock found during counting is not adjusted away. The affected pallets are labelled, segregated and moved to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found under PR-09, recorded with product, batch and location, and notified to the shift supervisor and stock control. The bay or face stays open only for correct stock.

9. All staff wear high-visibility vests and class S3 safety footwear during counts, and all moves observe 10 km/h inside the hall and 5 km/h at pedestrian zones, crossings and dock ramps. Counters do not climb racking, move racked pallets by hand, or enter the hazmat cage or Zone E except for a directed count task.

10. Every count, recount and exception is scan-recorded in the system before handover. Date, time, location, product, batch, counted quantity, checker names and investigation notes are entered in the shift record, and open discrepancies, quarantined lines and proposed adjustments are carried into the end-of-shift handover under PR-15 until approved and closed.

title: Annual Stocktake
text:
1. A full wall-to-wall stocktake of all inventory is carried out once a year under PR-08. It covers every pallet, carton and unit in Zone B bulk storage, Zone C pick faces, Zone E cold zone, Zone D staging where applicable, and the ventilated hazmat cage and quarantine in Zone F. No location is excluded or carried over.

2. The stocktake is a shutdown count. All receiving, put-away, replenishment, picking, packing and dispatch movements are stopped for the stocktake period, inbound Doors 1-4 and outbound Doors 5-8 are closed to flow, and Zone A is cleared of unbooked goods before counting starts. Only count, recount and safety staff move on the floor.

3. The date is planned in advance by the warehouse manager outside peak season. The manager defines the shutdown window, rosters the count teams from stock controllers, shift supervisors, inbound, picking and returns staff, and approves any overtime needed. Only the warehouse manager approves overtime for the stocktake.

4. Preparation is owned by the stock controllers under the manager. They freeze the system stock at cut-off, publish the location sequence for all 2,400 pallet positions in Zone B plus faces, cold store and cage, issue count sheets and scanner tasks on the 20 handheld WMS scanners, and ensure every location carries a readable label with product, quantity, batch and location.

5. Counts are worked by location in pairs, blind and independent. Each team scans the location, counts every pallet, carton and unit in place, checks product identity, batch, expiry where applicable, label and pallet condition, and records the quantity without seeing the system figure. The system stock is the stock on the rack, so only counted quantities count.

6. Bulk, cold and hazmat discipline applies through the count. Each rack bay is counted as found within its 2,700 kg bay limit built on the 1,000 kg maximum per pallet load included, block stacks within 3 pallets high and 4.0 m together, Zone E without breaking the +2 °C to +8 °C regime, and hazmat only in the 60 m2 cage within its 4,000 kg limit. Segregation is never broken to count.

7. No inventory adjustment is ever posted without a second count. Where the first count differs from the system, a different checker recounts the same location blind. Only two matching counts, or a supervised investigation that explains the difference, allow an adjustment to be proposed for approval.

8. Damaged or suspect stock found during the stocktake is not adjusted away. It is labelled, segregated and moved to quarantine in Zone F the same day it is found under PR-09, recorded with product, batch and location, and notified to the shift supervisor and stock control. No damaged line is counted as available stock.

9. Safety rules apply in full during the shutdown. Counters work in the 3.0 m rack storage aisles and at ground-level faces, keep 4.0 m main transport aisles clear, and use only the 1.2 m walkways behind yellow barriers on foot. All staff wear high-visibility vests and class S3 safety footwear, and any truck move observes 10 km/h inside and 5 km/h at pedestrian zones, crossings and ramps.

10. The stocktake is closed only by the warehouse manager. The stock controllers reconcile first and second counts, list all proposed adjustments with evidence, and present the results for manager review. The manager personally signs off the annual wall-to-wall stocktake results, and only then are approved adjustments booked. The signed results, count records and open quarantine lines are filed and carried into handover under PR-15.

title: Recounts and Adjustments
text:
1. No inventory adjustment is ever posted without a second count. A difference between the system quantity and the first count never becomes a booking on its own. The location stays open, the stock stays where it is, and the adjustment waits until the recount rule is met under PR-08.

2. A recount is triggered by any mismatch. Where the first count differs from the system figure, by overage, shortage, wrong product, wrong batch or damaged quantity, stock control orders an immediate blind recount of the same location before any other move to or from that bay or face.

3. Recounts are blind and independent. A different checker from the first count recounts the same zone, bay or face without seeing the first result, scanning the location and every pallet, carton and unit in place on the handheld WMS scanners. Product identity, batch, expiry where applicable, labels and pallet condition are checked again.

4. Only two matching counts allow an adjustment to be proposed. If the recount matches the first count, the stock controllers may propose an adjustment to the counted quantity with both records as evidence. If the two counts differ, a supervised investigation follows, including checks of adjacent locations, recent put-away, replenishment, picking and dispatch tasks.

5. Investigations are owned by the stock controllers with the shift supervisor. They trace scanner history, booking references, misplaced pallets, unconfirmed transfers and open quarantine lines in Zone F. No estimate is booked, and the system stock remains the stock on the rack until the true quantity is proven by count.

6. Damaged or suspect stock is never adjusted away. Pallets found damaged, leaking, unstable, overweight above 1,000 kg per pallet load included, or outside the +2 °C to +8 °C regime for chilled lines are labelled, segregated and moved to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found under PR-09. The adjustment proposal covers only correct stock.

7. Every proposed adjustment is recorded before approval. The proposal shows date, time, location in Zone B, Zone C, Zone E or the 60 m2 hazmat cage in Zone F, product, batch, system quantity, first and recount quantities, checker names, investigation notes and quarantine references. It is scan-recorded in the system as pending, not as available stock.

8. No adjustment is booked without approval. Proposals prepared by the stock controllers require approval before posting, with write-off values following the fixed split: the shift supervisor approves damaged-goods write-offs up to and including 500 EUR, and any write-off above 500 EUR and the annual wall-to-wall results are reserved to the warehouse manager. Unapproved quantities are never picked, replenished or dispatched.

9. Approved adjustments are booked at once and checked after. Stock controllers post the approved quantity, re-scan the location to confirm the new system figure matches the rack, and clear the location for normal put-away, replenishment and picking. Rejected proposals return for further recount and remain open in the shift record.

10. All recounts, investigations, proposals, approvals and postings are entered before handover under PR-15. Open discrepancies, pending approvals and quarantined lines are carried into the end-of-shift handover until closed. Counts are worked within mornings 06:00-14:00 and afternoons 14:00-22:00 in 3.0 m rack aisles and 4.0 m main aisles, on 1.2 m walkways behind yellow barriers, wearing high-visibility vests and class S3 footwear, observing 10 km/h inside and 5 km/h at pedestrian zones, crossings and ramps.

title: Returns Inspection
text:
1. All returns are received and inspected only in Zone F under PR-07. No return is unloaded directly to Zone B, Zone C, Zone D or Zone E, and no returned pallet or carton re-enters bulk, pick faces or dispatch without passing inspection in Zone F.

2. Returns vehicles are booked by the dispatcher with a specific door and time slot and report to the office annex on arrival. Drivers wait in the marked waiting area until called forward, and returned goods are moved promptly to the marked returns inspection area inside the 600 m2 Zone F services and control area.

3. Returns are accepted only within 14 days of delivery. Returns and packing staff check the original delivery reference, delivery date, customer, product and quantity against the delivery record and the return request. Any return outside the 14-day window, without a delivery reference, or without dispatcher and supervisor instruction is held separately and not inspected as a return.

4. Every returned unit is inspected, without sampling. Returns and packing staff open, count and check each carton and unit by product, quantity, batch and expiry where applicable, outer packaging, seal, labelling, pallet condition, and visible damage, leakage, contamination or temperature failure. No estimate or unchecked quantity passes forward.
